lead: This unit explains how spark-ignition and compression-ignition engines receive their fuel, and how spark-ignition engines make and time the spark. It moves from the carburettor to mechanical and electronic injection, gasoline direct injection, nozzles and sprays, governors, and battery, magneto, electronic and laser ignition. After it you can size a simple carburettor and an injection pump, work out injector pulses and spray penetration, and set spark advance.
about: The first chapter sets the petrol engine's mixture target and shows how a simple carburettor and its circuits meet it. The next three move to diesel injection: the requirements and types of injection with timing and lag, the jerk pump, distributor pump and unit injector, and the common rail, where pressure and timing are separated. Two chapters cover petrol injection: mono-point and multi-point electronic injection, then gasoline direct injection. The nozzle chapter follows the fuel into the cylinder as a spray, and the governor chapter shows how a diesel holds its speed by moving the fuel rack. The last three cover ignition: battery-coil and magneto systems, electronic and laser ignition, and spark timing and advance, which only a few syllabi list separately.

chapters.idea: A carburettor must vary the air-fuel ratio with load and speed, and separate circuits do that for idle, cruise, power and acceleration.

figure.title: Mixture target against load
figure.aria: A line graph of required air-fuel ratio against engine load, starting rich at idle, leaning at cruise, and becoming rich again at full load.

chapters.example: An engine takes 0.045 kg/s of air. The carburettor is set for 15:1 by mass. Petrol density is 750 kg/m³. Find fuel mass flow and volume flow. Fuel mass flow = 0.045/15 = 0.003 kg/s. Volume flow = 0.003/750 = 4×10⁻⁶ m³/s = 4 cm³/s.
chapters.trap: Thinking the main jet alone sets the mixture at all loads; acceleration and choke are extra-fuel circuits.

chapters.idea: A fuel injection system must meter, atomise, distribute and time fuel; its types are classified by air assist, direct or indirect injection, and control.

figure.aria: A classification tree of fuel injection systems, splitting into air injection and solid injection, then direct and indirect forms.

chapters.example: A four-cylinder four-stroke diesel engine uses 6 kg/h of fuel at 1800 rpm. Find the fuel delivered per injection per cylinder. 6 kg/h = 0.1 kg/min. Injections per cylinder per min = 1800/2 = 900. Total injections/min = 4×900 = 3600. Fuel per injection = 0.1/3600 = 2.78×10⁻⁵ kg = 27.8 mg.
chapters.trap: Confusing direct injection with direct control; forgetting four-stroke injection frequency is rpm/2 per cylinder.

chapters.idea: Mechanical diesel pumps generate injection pressure by plunger motion and time delivery by spill or distribution; unit injectors combine pump and nozzle at the cylinder.

figure.title: Jerk pump delivery
figure.aria: A block flow of a jerk pump: cam lift moves the plunger, the spill port closes, pressure opens the delivery valve, and the nozzle injects.

chapters.example: A jerk pump plunger has diameter 8 mm and effective stroke 3 mm. Find fuel delivered per injection. Area = π(0.008²)/4 = 5.027×10⁻⁵ m². Volume = 5.027×10⁻⁵×0.003 = 1.508×10⁻⁷ m³ = 150.8 mm³.
chapters.trap: Taking total plunger stroke as effective stroke; the spill port closes only after the inlet port is covered.

chapters.idea: Common rail stores fuel at high pressure in one rail and uses ECU-controlled injectors, so pressure and injection timing can be set independently.

figure.title: Common rail layout
figure.aria: A common-rail layout: fuel runs from tank through lift pump and filter to a high-pressure pump, then to a rail and injectors, with the ECU controlling rail pressure and injector timing.

chapters.example: An injector delivers 30 mm³ per injection. The engine is a four-cylinder four-stroke running at 3000 rpm. Find fuel flow in L/h. Injections per cylinder per min = 3000/2 = 1500. Total injections/min = 4×1500 = 6000. Volume/min = 30×6000 = 180000 mm³/min = 180 cm³/min = 0.18 L/min = 10.8 L/h.
chapters.trap: Saying rail pressure sets injection quantity alone; quantity depends on rail pressure and injector open time together.

chapters.idea: Electronic fuel injection uses sensors, an ECU and solenoid or piezo injectors to meter fuel; mono-point injects at the throttle body, multi-point at each port, and GDI injects directly into the cylinder.

figure.title: Electronic fuel injection loop
figure.aria: A closed-loop electronic fuel injection block diagram: sensors send signals to the ECU, which pulses injectors into the engine, and the O2 sensor feeds exhaust information back to the ECU.

chapters.example: An injector flows 240 cm³/min when fully open. It is held open for 5 ms. Find fuel delivered per injection. 240 cm³/min = 4 cm³/s. Volume = 4×0.005 = 0.02 cm³ = 20 mm³.
chapters.trap: Mixing up mono-point and multi-point locations; thinking GDI is the same as port injection.

chapters.idea: Gasoline direct injection sprays petrol into the cylinder at high pressure, giving charge cooling, a higher compression ratio and stratified lean running.
The nozzle turns fuel pressure into a spray; hole size, hole number, opening pressure and injection pressure set atomisation, penetration and cone angle.

figure.title: Nozzle spray chain
figure.aria: A block flow from high fuel pressure through a five-hole nozzle, where the jet breaks into droplets, penetrates the chamber and mixes with air.

chapters.example: A nozzle has 5 holes, each of diameter 0.25 mm. Find total flow area. Area per hole = π(0.00025²)/4 = 4.909×10⁻⁸ m². Total area = 5×4.909×10⁻⁸ = 2.454×10⁻⁷ m² = 0.245 mm².
chapters.trap: Using nozzle hole diameter instead of radius in the area formula; assuming more holes are always better without matching penetration and air motion.

chapters.idea: A governor holds engine speed by sensing speed and moving the fuel rack; mechanical centrifugal and pneumatic types are the common exam forms.

figure.title: Governor speed control loop
figure.aria: A governor control loop: set speed is compared by the governor, which moves the fuel rack, changing engine fuel and actual speed, which feeds back to the governor.

chapters.example: A centrifugal governor has a ball of mass 0.1 kg at radius 50 mm rotating at 1200 rpm. Find the centrifugal force on one ball. ω = 2π×1200/60 = 125.7 rad/s. F = mω²r = 0.1×125.7²×0.05 = 79.0 N.
chapters.trap: Thinking the governor sets fuel quantity directly; it sets speed by changing fuel, while quantity still depends on load.

chapters.idea: Battery-coil ignition takes energy from the battery and magneto ignition makes its own; both use an induction coil to produce the spark.

figure.title: Battery-coil ignition
figure.aria: A battery-coil ignition block diagram: battery current through the switch builds in the primary coil, the contact breaker interrupts it, the secondary coil sends high voltage to the distributor and spark plug.

chapters.example: A coil has primary inductance L = 6 mH and current I = 4 A at the instant the contact breaker opens. Find the stored energy. E = ½LI² = 0.5×0.006×16 = 0.048 J = 48 mJ.
chapters.trap: Saying a magneto needs a battery; confusing primary current with spark current.

chapters.idea: Electronic ignition replaces the contact breaker with a trigger and a transistor or thyristor; laser ignition replaces the electrodes with a focused laser pulse.
Spark timing must move earlier as speed rises and load falls, so spark advance is scheduled to get peak pressure near TDC without knock.

figure.title: Spark advance against speed
figure.aria: A line graph of spark advance against engine speed, rising from ten degrees at one thousand rpm to forty degrees at four thousand rpm.

chapters.example: At 1000 rpm the spark advance is 10°; at 3000 rpm it is 30°. Find the advance at 2500 rpm if the schedule is linear. Slope = (30° − 10°)/(3000 − 1000) = 20°/2000 rpm = 0.01°/rpm. Advance = 10° + (2500 − 1000)×0.01 = 25°.
chapters.trap: Thinking advance is fixed; high load needs retard to avoid knock, while high speed needs more advance.
